PhD thesis (Pacific Studies), Macmillan Brown Centre for Pacific Studies, University of Canterbury (Christchurch). c. 250 pp. (CORE work 171003111, UC Research Repository).
sources.note: No phonology content. Language material is limited to Luqa conflict/peace terminology (vaipera, vai raja, ira, kame, the reciprocal prefix vai- vs sa-) and one pragmatic remark that in emphatic speech 'the pe in vaipera is dragged out longer than the other syllables' (p. 157) -- expressive lengthening, not a word-stress statement. Speaker estimate 5,000-6,000 (citing Tabureguci 2012).

sources.citation: McDougall, Debra. 2016. Engaging with Strangers: Love and Violence in the Rural Solomon Islands (ASAO Studies in Pacific Anthropology 6). New York/Oxford: Berghahn Books. Front matter: 'Notes on Language, Orthography, and Names' (De Gruyter chapter DOI 10.1515/9781785330216-003; JSTOR j.ctvgs09mh). Read from the publisher's open 'Read Excerpt' (Jellybooks cloud reader, note.xhtml).
sources.note: Orthography and segmental pronunciation only: vowel values (a e i o u, ei au ae ai), consonants as in English, ny palatal nasal, r slightly trilled, 'In Luqa, z is often pronounced as /j/', 'All voiced stops are pre-nasalized in New Georgian languages' (b=mb, d=nd, j=nj, q=ngg), g = voiced velar fricative, ng = velar nasal, competing Methodist/Adventist spellings of velars; Luqa vs Kubokota differences (/z/~/s/, vari-~vai-, butubutu~bubutu). No word on stress, accent, tone or intonation.

sources.citation: Chambers, Mary Ruth. 2009. Which way is up? Motion verbs and paths of motion in Kubokota, an Austronesian language of the Solomon Islands. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London.
sources.note: Describes stress for KUBOKOTA (ghan1242, northern Ranongga), not Luqa: sec. 2.1.3 pp. 53-55, disyllabic trochaic feet parsed left to right, final leftover syllable extrametrical, primary stress on rightmost foot (initial stress in 2-3 syllable words), secondary stress on first and alternate syllables. Luqa/Lungga is treated only as the 'closely related' southern neighbour (pp. 21-22; 78.9% lexical similarity) with scattered lexical/morphological footnotes (e.g. Luqa reduplicates only the first syllable); no statement about Luqa stress.

sources.citation: Raymond, Mary [Mary Raymond Chambers]. n.d. [c. 2005-2008]. Luqa. Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database, language entry 509 (247 items, with notes on orthography and phonetics).
sources.note: Notes: 'Orthography: q = voiced velar stop, v = voiced bilabial fricative, ng = velar nasal, ny = palatal nasal, g = voiced velar fricative, j = voiced palatal affricate. All voiced stops and affricates are prenasalized.' No stress marks in the forms, no stress statement -- wordlist-only data.
